analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to regulate tobacco products, including ingredients, advertising, warning labels, and new products.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 84 cosponsors from both parties, but was sent to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee in June 2004 and never received a vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made tobacco products subject to federal regulation for the first time. Cigarette makers would have to register with the FDA each year, disclose every ingredient and harmful chemical in their products, and get approval before selling any new product. The FDA could set warning labels, restrict advertising that reaches young people, ban candy-flavored cigarettes, and recall dangerously harmful products. Congress would keep the power to ban products outright or force nicotine to zero.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, especially children who would face less tobacco advertising and fewer flavored products, current smokers who would get more accurate warnings and ingredient disclosure, and taxpayers who would save on tobacco-related health costs. The bill's own findings estimated that cutting youth smoking in half would keep more than 2 million of today's children from dying early and save roughly $75 billion in health care costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, smokers, and public health programs

how_it_helps.text: Tobacco use causes more than 400,000 deaths a year in the U.S. and about 8.6 million Americans have chronic illnesses related to smoking, according to the bill's findings.
The bill requires annual registration and inspection of tobacco manufacturers, disclosure of all ingredients and harmful constituents by brand, and user fees to fund FDA oversight.
It bans cigarettes with candy, fruit, spice, or other characterizing flavors — strawberry, cinnamon, clove, coffee and more — which appeal to new, young smokers, though menthol is exempted.
Every new tobacco product would need FDA premarket approval, and the FDA could require public notification and recalls of unreasonably harmful products.
The Secretary could restrict tobacco advertising and promotion when that protects public health, and the bill upgrades cigarette and smokeless tobacco warning label requirements.

The bill's findings state that reducing youth smoking by 50 percent would prevent more than 6.5 million of today's children from becoming regular smokers, saving over 2 million from premature death and roughly $75 billion in health care costs.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers would pay registration, inspection, recordkeeping, user fees, and compliance costs, and would face premarket review of new products and restrictions on how they advertise. Those costs would largely be passed on in cigarette prices, meaning smokers would pay more at the counter. Tobacco growers were explicitly carved out of the bill's reach.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco makers, and smokers through higher prices

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts menthol from its flavored-cigarette ban, leaving untouched the one flavor most associated with heavily marketed brands and with high smoking rates among Black Americans.

The bill caps the legal purchase age at 18, bars any rule that would ban sales by a category of retail outlets, and forbids requiring a doctor's authorization to buy tobacco — limits on how far the FDA could go.
It reserves to Congress the power to ban tobacco products outright or require nicotine to be reduced to zero, so the FDA itself could never take those steps.
FDA oversight is funded through industry user fees, a cost manufacturers would pass to consumers in cigarette prices.
Tobacco leaf growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives are exempted from the bill entirely; FDA employees could not even enter a tobacco farm without written consent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case was strong: an unregulated product that kills more than 400,000 Americans a year would come under ingredient disclosure, premarket review, advertising limits, and better warnings, with youth smoking as the main target. The honest weaknesses are the menthol carve-out — which protects a profitable product line while banning every other flavored cigarette — and the hard limits Congress placed on the FDA, including the 18-year-old minimum age and the inability to ban products or set nicotine to zero. Even with those compromises, this version was far tougher than nothing, which is what smokers and children got in the 108th Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, then to that committee's Health Subcommittee in June 2004, and it sat there with no markup or vote until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Davis (R-VA) introduced the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act on May 20, 2004, joined by Reps. Waxman, Platts, and Meehan.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On June 18, 2004, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken in the 108th Congress.
The bill attracted 84 cosponsors, 51 Democrats and 33 Republicans, but the committee never reported it and the House never voted on it.
The bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: for another Congress, they faced no federal registration, ingredient disclosure, premarket review, or advertising restrictions, and the industry's roughly $11 billion annual marketing budget — much of it aimed at young people — kept running unregulated.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan: 51 of 204 House Democrats and 33 of 229 House Republicans cosponsored, and the bill never reached a floor vote, so no party-line roll call was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill imposed real costs — registration, inspections, ingredient disclosure, user fees, premarket approval of new products, and advertising limits. But it also entrenched the biggest makers: compliance costs favor large firms over small ones, and Philip Morris publicly backed FDA regulation while smaller rivals fought it, viewing federal rules as a way to freeze market shares.

The flavored-cigarette ban explicitly excludes menthol, carving out the most heavily menthol-dependent part of the market from the bill's toughest provision while menthol products remain heavily marketed to Black communities.
Banning candy, fruit, and spice flavorings and requiring premarket approval of new products hits small and niche makers hardest, and their loss is the point of the public health benefit.

Growers, warehouses, and cooperatives are exempted from FDA authority entirely — FDA staff cannot even enter a tobacco farm without written consent — keeping the upstream of the supply chain outside federal health oversight.

industries.industry: Public health programs and health insurers
industries.note: Reducing youth smoking would cut future treatment costs; the bill's findings cite roughly $75 billion in health care savings from halving youth smoking.
